cases.abstract: Low-rank adaptation must encode changes in both the scale and direction of pretrained weights through the same matrix update. An analysis of VL-BART shows positively correlated magnitude and directional changes for LoRA, whereas full fine-tuning exhibits a negative correlation. Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) uses this observation to separate trainable column magnitudes from directions updated by low-rank factors. Normalizing the updated directions makes magnitude adjustment explicit, and the adapted weights can be merged before inference. Across eight commonsense reasoning tasks, DoRA raises LLaMA-7B's average accuracy from 74.7% to 78.4% at the same rank, with learning-rate adjustment and trainable fractions of 0.83% and 0.84%, respectively. A half-rank configuration achieves 77.5% while training 0.43% of parameters. Multimodal evaluations also favor DoRA over LoRA, but its VL-BART video-task average remains below full fine-tuning. The implementation detaches normalization denominators to control training overhead; a LLaMA-7B ablation reduces memory by 24.4% with a 0.2-point accuracy decrease. Together, these comparisons show that a separate magnitude vector can improve the accuracy obtained from a restricted directional update budget.
cases.methods: DoRA represents each adapted weight column as a learned magnitude multiplied by a normalized direction. The direction is obtained by adding a low-rank matrix product to the frozen pretrained weights; the magnitude vector is initialized from their column norms, and the low-rank product starts at zero. Consequently, adaptation begins from the original model while assigning scale changes to a small separate parameter vector. This separation lets the low-rank factors alter direction without also having to encode every magnitude adjustment. The practical training procedure recomputes the normalization denominator but detaches it during backpropagation, avoiding the additional gradient graph required by exact normalization. This retains the forward reparameterization and magnitude gradient, but replaces the exact direction gradient's projection with a scaling operation. After training, the normalized and rescaled weights are merged for deployment.
cases.results: On the eight commonsense tasks, LLaMA-7B reaches 78.4% average accuracy with DoRA, compared with 74.7% for LoRA, while the trainable fractions differ only from 0.83% to 0.84%. These same-rank configurations use an adjusted learning rate for DoRA, so the comparison assesses the adaptation recipe rather than isolating decomposition under identical optimization settings. Halving DoRA's rank still yields 77.5% with 0.43% of parameters trainable, showing that the improvement need not depend on increasing the adaptation budget. The advantage does not imply that DoRA reproduces full fine-tuning across modalities: VL-BART's reported video-task average improves from 83.5 with LoRA to 85.4 with DoRA but remains below 87.5 with full fine-tuning. The weight analysis offers a complementary observation, with magnitude-direction correlations of -0.31 for DoRA, -0.62 for full fine-tuning, and 0.83 for LoRA. This pattern is consistent with less tightly coupled adjustments, but is not itself a causal explanation of the benchmark gains.
cases.notes: Accuracy differences are percentage points. Multimodal task averages combine different metrics and are not labeled accuracy. Correlations are descriptive. The detached-normalization implementation is distinguished from the exact gradient analysis. Commonsense baselines for LLaMA-7B/13B were imported from prior work, and DoRA's learning rate was adjusted. Merging weights supports the absence of added adaptation operations at inference, not a measured speedup.

cases.abstract: GaLore reduces optimizer memory for language-model training by compressing gradients instead of constraining weights to a low-rank parameterization. Gradients are projected into a compact subspace, processed by an optimizer there, and mapped back to update the full weight matrix. Periodically refreshing the projection allows accumulated updates to span multiple subspaces. For structured gradient dynamics, the analysis bounds stable rank and gives a conditional convergence result for fixed projections without adaptive regularization. C4 pretraining experiments compare GaLore with full-rank optimization and low-rank alternatives, while fine-tuning experiments examine adaptation of pretrained models. In a single 7B run on 64 A100 GPUs over 19.7 billion tokens, 8-bit GaLore reaches validation perplexity 14.65 versus 14.61 for 8-bit Adam. Separately, combining projection, 8-bit optimizer states, and per-layer updates gives a measured 22.0 GB footprint at a small token batch size, without offloading or activation checkpointing, fitting within 24 GB capacity. These measurements establish a memory-saving option for full-weight training, with a throughput cost in the tested implementation.
cases.methods: For a weight matrix, GaLore takes a singular value decomposition of the current gradient and retains a rank-limited projection. The implementation projects on one side of the gradient, choosing that side from the matrix dimensions, so Adam's first and second moments occupy the reduced space. The processed update is then mapped back and added directly to the full weight matrix. Recomputing the projection periodically prevents training from remaining confined to one fixed update subspace; accumulated updates can therefore reach beyond a single low-rank factorization. This targets optimizer-state storage without introducing trainable adapters. The theoretical convergence result applies instead to fixed projections with no adaptive regularizer: it contracts the projected gradient when curvature in the retained subspace exceeds the stated continuity-dependent threshold and the learning rate yields contraction. That result describes progress within a designated subspace, not a convergence guarantee for the switching Adam implementation.
cases.results: At the 1B scale on C4, rank-512 GaLore obtains validation perplexity 15.64 after 13.1 billion training tokens, close to the full-rank baseline's 15.56 and below LoRA's 19.21 at the same rank. Its estimated weight-and-optimizer storage is 4.38 GB, compared with 7.80 GB for full-rank training and 6.17 GB for LoRA. This comparison supports compressing update statistics while retaining full weights, rather than assigning the memory benefit to a smaller model. Actual device savings also depend on scheduling: the 7B footprint of 22.0 GB combines low-rank projection with 8-bit states and immediate per-layer updates, at a small per-device token batch size. These savings are not cost-free. In a reported 1B measurement at a token batch size of 256, throughput falls from 1205.31 tokens per second with 8-bit Adam to 1019.63 with 8-bit GaLore, while memory falls from 6.93 to 5.63 GB. GaLore thus trades some throughput for reduced storage rather than improving both simultaneously.
cases.notes: The 7B quality comparison is one untuned trial on 64 A100 GPUs; the 22.0 GB measurement establishes capacity feasibility, not equivalent training on a consumer GPU. Parameter-and-optimizer estimates are kept separate from actual device memory. Fixed-projection convergence does not certify switching Adam or decay of the full gradient. Throughput values use corresponding Table 11 rows without interpreting its ambiguous layer-wise labels. Fine-tuning gains are mixed: GLUE averages remain below full fine-tuning, and GaLore's OpenAssistant perplexity on LLaMA-7B is slightly worse than LoRA's.
